papers.title_in_file: Quantum Systems for Monte Carlo Methods and Applications to Fractional Stochastic Processes
papers.version_note: arXiv:1810.05639v1 [quant-ph], 11 Oct 2018; preprint submitted to Elsevier, October 16, 2018.
papers.what_it_is: A preprint that uses a photonic quantum random number generator as the random source for Monte Carlo simulation of fractional Brownian motion and for pricing target volatility options under the fractional SABR model, and compares it with pseudo-random numbers.

assertions.value: The authors state that their quantum random number generator is based on measuring the arrival times of single photons in shaped temporal modes (Figure 1), and that the device is presented in their earlier paper [22].
quotes: In a recent paper [22], we present a viable source of unbiased quantum random numbers whose
The device is based on measuring the arrival times of single photons in shaped temporal modes, as illustrated in Figure 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own device principle in Section 2.1.
assertions.reader_inference: This paper only gives the Figure 1 caption and a one-sentence principle; the laser, modulator and detector details are in reference [22], not in this text.

assertions.value: The authors state that their generator can produce samples with any preassigned distribution, and a figure shows histograms for a modified Bessel distribution and an arbitrary distribution; that figure is stated to be a reproduction of Figure 2 in [22].
quotes: our QRN generator can produce samples with any preassigned distribution
We note that our QRN generator can produce samples in real–time from any given distribution with high speed and accuracy.
is a reproduction of Figure 2 in [22].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the evidence is a figure reproduced from an earlier paper [22].
assertions.reader_inference: The distribution flexibility is shown here only through a reproduced figure; no distribution-fit statistic is given in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QRN data used for the tests contains 2.07732758 × 108 (printed flat; two point zero seven seven three two seven five eight times ten to the eighth) random integers, written on 32 bits.
quotes: The data (QRNs) contains 2.07732758 × 108 random integers in the set
written on 32 bits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test-data setup in Section 2.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say how many QRNs were drawn for the fBM and option-pricing runs (see the Table 2 assertion).

assertions.value: The authors state that the generated numbers are uniformly distributed, with the histogram and normalized histogram given in Figure 2.
quotes: The histogram and the normalized histogram of the sample are given in Figure 2.
Note that the generated numbers are uniformly distributed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A visual histogram result from one sample; no goodness-of-fit statistic is quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Ziggurat algorithm or the Box–Muller transform converts the uniform distribution to a standard normal one. In the caption's example a sample of 2 × 108 (printed flat; two times ten to the eighth) uniformly distributed integers was transformed in C++ on a 2.4 GHz 6-Core Intel Xeon Processor, with execution times 173.011 seconds (Box–Muller) and 142.731 seconds (Ziggurat), respectively.
quotes: By applying the Ziggurat algorithm or the Box–Muller transform, one can transform the uniform distribution into a standard normal distribution.
Probability density functions obtained from a sample of 2 × 108 uniformly distributed random integers via Box–Muller and Ziggurat transform, respectively.
The algorithms were implemented in C++ on a 2.4 GHz 6-Core Intel Xeon Processor.
The execution time is 173.011 and 142.731 seconds, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single timing run on one machine.
assertions.reader_inference: The order of the two times follows the order of the two algorithms in the caption. This is the only timing in the paper; no run time of the fBM path generation or of the option pricing is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that generating normally distributed samples is straightforward from the experimental point of view, which makes preprocessing or transformation of their data unnecessary.
quotes: In particular, generating normally distributed samples is straightforward from the experimental point of view which makes preprocessing/transformation of our data unnecessary.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a measurement in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No result in this paper shows normal samples drawn directly from the device; the randomness tests are on uniform integers. The paper does not say whether the QRNs used in the fBM and pricing runs were native normal samples or transformed uniforms.

assertions.value: The authors report that the NIST tests [25] and Dieharder tests were applied to their QRNs, and that to repeat a test that returned weak they used the option -Y 1 in the Dieharder routine, also known as resolve ambiguity mode.
quotes: The NIST tests [25] and Dieharder tests1,2 were applied to our QRNs.
we used the option -Y 1 in the Dieharder routine, also known as
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test procedure in Section 2.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Re-running tests that return weak means the reported pass counts are after re-testing; the paper does not report how many tests were weak on the first run.

assertions.value: The authors state that their QRNs pass all Dieharder tests for randomness, and that they pass the NIST and Dieharder suites without any randomness extraction; the Dieharder p-value figure is stated to be a reproduction of Figure 2 in [22].
quotes: pass all standard randomness tests of the NIST and Dieharder test suites without any randomness extraction
our QRNs pass all Dieharder tests for randomness
Note that our QRNs pass all the statistical tests from the Dieharder test suite.
is a reproduction of Figure 2 in [22].
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Passing statistical test suites is consistent with randomness but does not establish that the numbers are truly random.

assertions.value: Table 1 lists a NIST pass rate of 15/15 for each of six sources: QuEST Lab, ANU 1, ANU 2, IDQ (web data), IDQ Quantis Device 1 and IDQ Quantis Device 2.
quotes: QuEST Lab ANU 1 ANU 2 IDQ (web data) IDQ Quantis Device 1 IDQ Quantis Device 2
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The column order of the flattened table text is read as the order of the sources in the header line.

quotes: QuEST Lab ANU 1 ANU 2 IDQ (web data) IDQ Quantis Device 1 IDQ Quantis Device 2
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The ANU 1 sample also passes 31/31, equal to the authors' device. The two device samples differ greatly in size (see the Table 1 sample-size assertion).

assertions.value: The comparison table reports data sizes of 830.9, 1050, 104.9, 125, 100 and 100 MB, and sample sizes (32-bit integers) of 2.077, 2.621, 0.262, 0.3125, 0.25 and 0.25 times ten to the eighth (exponents printed flat), for the six sources in header order; all six distributions are listed as Uniform.
assertions.certainty_reason: Table 1 states the sizes of the samples compared.
assertions.reader_inference: The samples compared are of unequal size, and the authors' sample is the second-largest in sample count except for ANU 1; pass rates are therefore not from equal-length streams.

By comparison, the IDQ numbers fail some Dieharder tests.
The ANU numbers have similar quality as SIT QRNs, the only major
assertions.certainty_reason: An author comparison from one study; part of it is not borne out by Table 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that ANU has 5.7 Gbits/sec, while they can generate at 8 Gbits/sec.
quotes: (ANU has 5.7 Gbits/sec, while we can generate at 8 Gbits/sec)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no measurement described in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say whether the 8 Gbits/sec rate was the rate used in the fBM and pricing runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is well known that pseudo-random number generators are not random at all, such that seed-based generators can produce identical strings of random numbers from the same seed and similar computational systems.
quotes: It is well known that pseudo-random number (PRN) generators are not random at all such that seed-based generators can be used to generate identical strings of random numbers based on the same seed and similar computational systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivating statement without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Determinism of a seeded generator is true by construction; the sentence does not show that PRN-driven Monte Carlo is less accurate.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [16], that it has been shown that the entropy rate also approaches zero when viable random seeds are used up.
quotes: Furthermore, it has been shown that the entropy rate also approaches zero when viable random seeds are used up [16].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to reference [16].

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum random numbers are physically created by quantum processes that are inherently stochastic, so that one cannot predict a sequence of numbers before they are acquired from the source, even with full knowledge of the state of the system.
quotes: In contrast, quantum random numbers (QRN) are physically created by quantum processes that are inherently stochastic.
even if one has full knowledge about the state of the system.
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivating statement without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, compared with other implementations that focus on data rate and test suite scores, their approach is notable because they also demonstrate that QRNs can be generated directly in arbitrary probability distributions, with high-dimensionality, and free of post-processing.
quotes: our approach is notable where we also demonstrate that QRNs can be generated directly in arbitrary probability distributions, with high-dimensionality, and free of post-processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; this paper shows no high-dimensional sample.
assertions.reader_inference: No result in this paper demonstrates high-dimensionality; any support is in reference [22].

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that the results indicate that, using the same number of random units, their QRNs achieve greater accuracy than those produced by standard pseudo-random number generators.
quotes: using the same number of random units, our QRNs achieve greater accuracy than those produced by standard pseudo-random number generators
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not name the pseudo-random generator, give a seed, or report repeated runs or confidence intervals, so the size of the difference relative to run-to-run variation is not shown.

assertions.value: The paper defines a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H in (0, 1) as a zero mean Gaussian process with the temporal covariance gamma(s, t) equal to one half of (t to the power 2H plus s to the power 2H minus |t − s| to the power 2H), for all s, t ≥ 0.
quotes: a fractional Brownian motion (fBM) with Hurst parameter H ∈ (0, 1) is a zero mean Gaussian process W H = {WtH , t ≥ 0} with a temporal covariance function given by
t2H + s2H − |t − s|2H
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definition it uses in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that it can be shown that a normalized fractional Brownian motion with H in (0, 1) is uniquely characterized by stationary increments, W0H = 0, mean zero, variance t to the power 2H for all t ≥ 0, and a Gaussian distribution for t > 0.
quotes: It can be shown that a normalized fractional Brownian motion {WtH }t≥0 with H ∈ (0, 1) is uniquely characterized by the following properties:
(i) WtH has stationary increments (ii) W0H = 0, E[WtH ] = 0, Var(WtH ) = E[(WtH )2] = t2H , ∀t ≥ 0 (iii) WtH has a Gaussian distribution for t > 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard fact stated without proof or citation here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the trajectories of the fractional Brownian motion are almost surely locally α-Hölder continuous for all α in (0, H), and state a displayed deduction from (1) that the expectation of the absolute increment equals |t − s| to the power 2H.
quotes: From (1) we deduce that
E[|WtH − WsH |] = |t − s|2H
the trajectories of W H are almost surely locally α−H¨older continuous for
all α ∈ (0, H).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a proof in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The displayed identity as printed is the first absolute moment; the covariance (1) gives the second moment E[(WtH − WsH)^2] = |t − s|^(2H). The printed form is probably a missing square, so it should be checked before the value is relied on.

assertions.value: The authors state that the fractional Brownian motion is not a semi-martingale nor Markovian (printed 'if H = 1/2', a sign that is probably a lost not-equal), so Itô stochastic calculus cannot be used with respect to it, and name the Skorokhod integral in Malliavin calculus [24], [4] and the pathwise Riemann-Stieltjes integral [27] as alternatives.
quotes: Since W H is not a semi-martingale nor Markovian if H = 1/2, we cannot use the
integral deﬁned in the framework of the Malliavin calculus [24], [4], or the pathwise Riemann-
Stieltjes integral [27].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of known theory with citations, not proved here.
assertions.reader_inference: For H = 1/2 the process is ordinary Brownian motion (the paper says W is recovered at H = 1/2), so the printed equals sign must mean not equal.

assertions.value: The authors report implementing two fractional Brownian motion simulation methods: the Davies and Harte method (originally from [11], detailed in Section 2.1.3 of [12]) and the hybrid scheme for Brownian semistationary processes of [5] using the Molchan–Golosov kernel; they state that fBM paths for the QRN versus PRN comparison are generated via the hybrid scheme.
quotes: The Davies and Harte method for generating fBM samples
The algorithm was originally proposed by [11] and it is presented in detail in Section 2.1.3 of [12].
The hybrid scheme for Brownian semistationary processes given in [5] was used to generate sample paths for fBMs
Fractional BM paths are generated via the hybrid scheme using both QRNs and PRNs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states which algorithms its simulations used.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not name the pseudo-random number generator or the transform used to make the PRN normals, nor how the QRN normals were produced.

assertions.value: The authors state that test routines for moments and errors were implemented: the mean and variance as functions of time via Monte Carlo, a chi-square test for fractional Gaussian noise, and the 2D correlation structure from sample paths.
quotes: In order to evaluate the algorithms, several test routines calculating moments and errors for fractional processes have been implemented:
as well as the 2D correlation structure γMC via sample paths:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation setup.
assertions.reader_inference: No result of the chi-square test is reported anywhere in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper defines three errors, epsilon 1, epsilon 2 and epsilon 3, as root mean squared errors with respect to the first two moments and the covariance in time of the simulated fBM paths: the mean over time points of the squared Monte Carlo mean, the mean of the squared difference between the Monte Carlo variance and t to the power 2H, and the mean of the squared difference between the Monte Carlo covariance and the exact covariance gamma(tk, tj).
quotes: To measure our QRNs performance, we introduce the following errors:
Note that εi, i = 1, 2, 3 are the root mean squared errors with respect to the
two moments and covariance in time of our simulated fBM paths.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines these error measures in Section 3.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the square roots in equations (7)-(9), so the exact placement of the roots is read from the sentence that calls them root mean squared errors. These errors compare to exact known moments, which is a sound benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors report generating fBM paths with H = 0.2 and T = 1 year and n = 252 samples, using the Davies and Harte method with 106 (printed flat; ten to the sixth) paths in one figure and the hybrid scheme with N = 50, 000 paths in two others, and state that by inspection the generated sample paths have the required properties of fBMs.
quotes: Parameters are H = 0.2, T = 1 year, n = 252 samples, N = 106 paths.
Parameters are H = 0.2, T = 1 year, n = 252 samples, N = 50, 000 paths.
By inspection, we notice that the generated sample paths have the required properties
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative inspection result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Figures 6 and 7 use PRNs; the checks are visual and no numeric error is reported for them.

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, one run per cell as far as the paper says.
assertions.reader_inference: At every N the QRN epsilon 1 and epsilon 2 are lower than the PRN values; QRN at N = 100,000 (0.00071814, 0.00105875) is below PRN at N = 500,000 (0.00079351, 0.00118751). The PRN epsilon 1 and epsilon 2 at N = 1,000,000 are identical (0.00063936), which looks like a copy error. The table lists no H, T or n; Figure 10 gives H = 0.1, T = 0.5, n = 500. The paper reports no repeats, seeds or confidence intervals, and does not name the PRN generator. A run with N = 1,000,000 paths of n = 500 steps needs at least 5 × 10^8 normal variates, more than the 2.07732758 × 10^8 integers the paper describes; how many QRNs were drawn is not said.

assertions.value: The error table reports epsilon three (covariance error) for PRN as 0.08907148, 0.08883075, 0.08904862, 0.08925236 and 0.08935881 at N = 10,000, 50,000, 100,000, 500,000 and 1,000,000, and for QRN as 0.030099337, 0.030027625, 0.030092520, 0.030153221 and 0.030184910 at the same N; the authors state that epsilon 3(N) is almost constant but that QRNs provide superior results.
quotes: The function ε3(N ) is almost constant, but we note once again that QRNs provide superior results.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: A covariance error that does not fall with N for either source (about 0.089 for PRN, about 0.030 for QRN) points to a systematic error in the path scheme or its implementation rather than to sampling noise; a roughly three-fold gap between two random sources feeding one scheme is not explained in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QRN rate of convergence is superior to its classical counterpart, thus yielding similar performance with fewer random samples (plots with H = 0.1, T = 0.5 and n = 500).
quotes: We note that the QRN rate of convergence is superior to its classical counterpart, thus yielding similar performance with less random samples.
Plot corresponds to Table 2. Parameters are H = 0.1, T = 0.5, n = 500.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: No convergence rate (slope) is fitted or reported; the claim rests on the Table 2 values and the Figure 10 curves.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is clear that the execution time is smaller when using QRNs, since no post-processing algorithm is applied and the random numbers are fed in real time to the path generation algorithm.
quotes: Moreover, it is clear that the execution time is smaller when using QRNs, since no post-processing algorithm is applied
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no timing of the path generation is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no wall-clock time for the QRN or PRN fBM runs. The speed advantage rests on skipping the transform step (Figure 3 timings) and on a real-time feed whose throughput in this experiment is not stated.

assertions.value: A comparison figure shows fBM mean and variance for PRN with N = 100,000 versus QRN with N = 25,000, and for PRN with N = 25,000 versus QRN with N = 25,000; the authors state that similar accuracy may be obtained with a smaller number of MC trials.
quotes: MC via PRN with N = 100,000 MC via QRN with N = 25,000
MC via PRN with N = 25,000 MC via QRN with N = 25,000
It is easy to notice that similar accuracy may be obtained with a smaller number of MC trials.
assertions.certainty_reason: A visual comparison from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is by eye from plots; no error number is reported for these N.

quotes: The analysis presented in this section is based on [14], where the authors propose the so–called
behaves like a fBM with Hurst exponent of order 0.1.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to reference [14].

assertions.value: The paper states the model from the cited work as sigma t equal to sigma 0 times exp of X t, with the log volatility driven by dXt = ν dWtH − α(Xt − m)dt, X0 = x0 > 0, with m a real number and α, ν, σ0 positive parameters, and states that choosing the fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process for the log volatility ensures a stationary model.
quotes: σt = σ0 exp{Xt}
dXt = νdWtH − α(Xt − m)dt, X0 = x0 > 0,
with m ∈ R, and α, ν, σ0 as positive parameters.
ensures a stationary model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the model it uses, taken from [14].

assertions.value: The authors report a full circle calibration check: they simulated one fBM path with their QuEST QRN generator using H = 0.14, built the fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck log-volatility path, and estimated H = 0.1354 from the slope of the scaling exponent against q, H = 0.1121 by the difference variance method and H = 0.1385 by the Peng method.
quotes: (i) Initialize the parameters and simulate one path of fBM using QuEST QRN generator.
From our simulations, we obtained H = 0.1354 (in order to generate the sample path, we used H = 0.14).
We obtain H = 0.1121 and H = 0.1385, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulated path.
assertions.reader_inference: Against the true value 0.14 the three errors are about 0.0046, 0.0279 and 0.0015 (reader arithmetic). Only one path is used and no PRN comparison is given for this estimation, so it does not show an advantage of QRN.

assertions.value: The authors state that their method is more efficient from a numerical point of view than its classical counterpart that uses pseudo-random numbers generated on a classical computer.
quotes: We indicate here that our method is more eﬃcient from a numerical point of view than its classical counterpart
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a timing result.
assertions.reader_inference: No wall-clock or per-path cost comparison is given in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the photonic quantum system produced truly random numbers that passed all standard randomness tests such as NIST and Dieharder, and that the efficiency, accuracy and execution time of the QRNs were demonstrated by rapid convergence and robustness in simulating fractional Brownian motion, a non-Markovian process with strict scaling properties.
quotes: The photonic quantum system used here produced truly random numbers that passed all standard randomness tests such as NIST and Dieharder.
a highly nontrivial stochastic process being both non-Markovian while maintaining strict scaling properties.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The execution-time part of the conclusion has no timing result in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results can be easily generalized and conjecture that QRN Monte Carlo trials for path dependent exotic options and multi-asset correlated options will be computationally less expensive and more accurate; they list multi-dimensional correlated paths, portfolio risk analysis and regulatory risk calculations (Basel III, CVA, XVA) as future applications, and state that QRNs showing their true strength under such scenarios is future research.
quotes: The results of this paper can be easily generalized: we conjecture that QRN MC trials for path dependent-exotic options and multi-asset correlated options will turn out to be computationally less expensive and more accurate.
enterprise wide regulatory risk calculations (Basel III, CVA, XVA, etc., see [8]) require and enormous amounts of multi-dimensional correlated simulation paths following arbitrary distributions.
QRN will show their true strength under such pricing scenarios which is a future research.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper itself states these as future work in Section 5.
assertions.reader_inference: The multi-asset, correlated and exotic cases are untested in this paper; only the one-asset fBM and target volatility options are run.
